title: Three days
hookLine: mourning is three days, and a widow's waiting period is longer (Bukhari)

lines: I HAVE NO NEED OF IT.
cards: News came to Umm Habibah, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: her father had died. She waited. On the third day, she called for perfume, a yellowish scent, and rubbed some on her arms and face.

Then she explained, in paraphrase: I have no need of perfume. But I heard the Prophet say that a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day should not mourn anyone more than three days, except a husband.
Zaynab bint Abi Salamah tells it, in Sahih al-Bukhari. A daughter who has just lost her father, putting on perfume, on purpose.

teach.b: The perfume was a signal: the outward mourning is finished. The hadith speaks to a believing woman. For three days, grief is given room, and adornment like perfume is set aside.
Then, by the Prophet's word, that outward season closes. Umm Habibah wasn't saying she'd stopped missing her father; she said plainly she had no need of the perfume. She was honoring the limit.
So there's permission here: grief gets real time, and three days is not a moment. And there's a boundary: the formal mourning doesn't swallow a life whole.

teach.h: A LONGER WAITING FOR A WIDOW.
teach.b: The hadith names one exception, a widow, and the Qur'an gives that waiting its own measure.

In surah al-Baqarah, women whose husbands have died wait, keeping to themselves, four months and ten days, and then, the verse says, there's no blame on them for what they decide for themselves in a fitting way.
That period is the 'iddah. Some readers see it as longer because more has ended: a household, a marriage, a whole shape of life.
So there are two clocks, a short one for a relative and a longer one for the person whose life was most rearranged. Neither says the love has stopped.

teach.h: A CONTAINER WITH A DOOR OUT.
teach.b: They give grief a container, with a beginning, a middle and a door out, and the people around know when to come close and when to let the grieving rise.

how: Muslims observe a period of mourning for a relative, which a hadith in al-Bukhari limits to three days, while a widow keeps a longer waiting period, the 'iddah, described in Qur'an 2:234

o: the limit of outward mourning for a relative, in the hadith
the widow's full waiting period after her husband dies
the wait before a burial, so relatives can travel in

p: put on perfume on the third day

s: Umm Habibah put on perfume because she wanted to
she said she had no need of it; she was honoring the Prophet's limit.
in the hadith, a widow's mourning is the exception to three days
the hadith names the husband as the exception.
the end of mourning means the love has ended
the clocks close the outward mourning; nothing in them says the love stops.

games.q: you're Umm Habibah. your father died days ago, and it's the third day. what do you do?
o: keep mourning as long as you feel like it.
call for perfume and put some on.
pretend nothing happened from day one.
games.why: she put on perfume on the third day, saying she had no need of it, to keep the Prophet's three-day limit.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has lost a person, recently or long ago, and picture sitting beside them: no advice, no fixing, just being there. Notice how much the sitting itself can say.
If you pray, you can remember them and the one they lost. If grief ever brings thoughts of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Three days. The time of outward mourning for a relative in the hadith, with a longer waiting, the 'iddah, for a widow. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the waiting period, here a widow's, set in al-Baqarah.

carryVoice: Your line: three days of mourning. Grief gets real time, and a door out. Go gently.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1280–1281 (Umm Habibah's perfume; mourning three days except for a husband)
Qur'an 2:234 (widows wait four months and ten days)
